apparatus: Jn 14:23 co-reigning; kingdom of God (hegemonikon state) vs of Christ (words/works).

choices.why: eunomoumenēn = under good law; the saint dwells in himself as a city under God's spiritual laws.
theopoieō = make divine; the praying disposition is god-made by the Word — theosis in prayer.

pass_a_gloss: Kingdom comes unobserved because within: pray its rise/fruit/perfection in self-as-city under Father and co-reigning Christ. God's kingdom = blessed hegemonikon-state; Christ's = saving words and righteous works. The always-pray objection dissolves via partial-knowledge: pray ever for more, journeying to the summit when Christ delivers the kingdom that God be all in all. Incompatibility with sin's kingdom; mortify, bear Spirit-fruit, walk paradise, seat Christ at the right hand within until death the last enemy falls and corruptible wears incorruption.
pass_b_english: 'Thy kingdom come.' The 'kingdom of God,' according to the word of our Lord and Savior, 'comes not with observation,' (1 Corinthians 15:50–55) 'nor shall they say: Lo here, or lo there' (Luke 17:20–21) — but 'the kingdom of God is within' us ('for the word is very nigh, in our mouth and in our heart' (Deuteronomy 30:14)). So it is plain that the one who prays for God's kingdom to come rightly prays concerning God's kingdom in himself — that it rise and bear fruit and be perfected. For every saint is ruled by God and obeys God's spiritual laws, dwelling in himself as in a well-ordered city — with the Father present to him, and Christ co-reigning with the Father in the perfected soul, according to the saying I recalled not long ago: 'We will come to him and make our abode with him.' (John 14:23) And I suppose God's kingdom is recognized as the blessed state of the ruling faculty and the ordered rank of wise reasonings, and Christ's kingdom as the progressive words, saving to their hearers, and the works of righteousness performed, and of the other virtues — for the Son of God is Word and Righteousness. But every sinner is tyrannized by the 'ruler of this age,' since every sinner is owned by the present evil age, not offering himself to him who 'gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from the present evil age' (Galatians 1:4) — and he 'delivers' 'according to the will of our God and Father,' (Romans 6:12) according to what is said in Galatians. And he who is tyrannized by this ruler of the age is ruled by sin by the voluntariness of his sinning. That is why Paul orders us no longer to submit when sin wills to rule us, commanding through these words: 'Let not sin, then, reign in your mortal body, to obey its lusts.' (1 Corinthians 12:8; 13:9–12)

But someone will say, to both — both the 'Hallowed be thy name' and the 'Thy kingdom come' — that if the pray-er prays to be heard, and is heard at some point, then plainly at some point God's 'name' shall be hallowed for someone, as aforesaid, and God's 'kingdom' shall stand in him. And if these things shall be his, how will he still becomingly pray concerning things present as though not present, saying 'Hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come' (Philippians 3:13)? And if so, will there ever be a time when it is not becoming to say 'Hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come' (1 Corinthians 15:24–28, 50–55)? We must say to this that, as one who prays to obtain a 'word of knowledge' and a 'word of wisdom' becomingly prays concerning these things always — always receiving, as he is heard, more contemplations of 'wisdom' and 'knowledge,' yet knowing 'in part' whatever at present he can hold, with the perfect, which annuls 'the partial,' 'then' to be revealed, when mind without sense assails the realities 'face to face' — so the perfect, both of hallowing God's 'name' in each of us and of his kingdom standing in him, cannot be unless the perfect 'come' also concerning 'knowledge' and 'wisdom' — and perhaps concerning the other virtues too. We journey toward perfection if we 'press toward the things before, forgetting the things behind.' (2 Corinthians 6:14–15) To God's kingdom in us, then, the summit shall stand as we advance without ceasing — when what the Apostle said is fulfilled: that Christ, when all enemies are subjected to him, 'shall deliver the kingdom to God the Father, that God may be all in all.' (Colossians 3:5) That is why, praying 'without ceasing,' with a disposition made godlike by the Word, we say to our Father in the heavens: 'Hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come.' (Galatians 5:22)

But concerning God's kingdom this too must be examined: that as there is no 'partnership of righteousness with lawlessness,' (Psalm 110:1) nor 'fellowship of light with darkness,' nor 'concord of Christ with Beliar' — so the kingdom of sin cannot co-exist with God's kingdom. If, then, we wish to be ruled by God, let 'sin in no way reign in our mortal body,' (1 Corinthians 13:9–12) nor let us obey its commands, when it calls our soul to 'the works of the flesh' and things foreign to God. But 'mortifying our members on earth,' let us bear the fruits 'of the Spirit,' that as in a spiritual 'paradise' the Lord may walk in us, ruling us alone with his Christ — seated 'at his right hand' in us, from whom we pray to receive spiritual 'power' — and seated, 'until' all his enemies in us become 'the footstool of his feet,' and every principality and authority and power be annulled from us. For these things can come to be in each of us, and the last enemy be annulled — death — so that in us too it be said by Christ: 'O death, where is thy sting? O Hades, where is thy victory?' (1 Corinthians 15:24–28) Now, then, let our 'corruptible put on' holiness in continence and all purity, and 'incorruption' — and our 'mortal' be clothed, death being annulled, with the Father's 'incorruption' — so that, ruled by God, we may already be in the goods of regeneration and resurrection.
